title: From Ocean Trash to Pavement: Hawaii's Recycled Plastic Roads
summary: Hawaii's pristine beaches belie a dirty secret: the islands are drowning in plastic waste. Recycling is costly and logistically challenging, and massive amounts of marine debris — especially abandoned fishing gear — keep washing ashore. Now, researchers are pioneering a solution that could turn this environmental headache into a literal road to sustainability. At the spring meeting of the American Chemical Society, Jeremy Axworthy of Hawaiʻi Pacific University's Center for Marine Debris Research (CMDR) presented findings on using recycled plastics in asphalt. “This work investigates whether it's responsible to use recycled plastics in Hawaii's roads,” Axworthy said. “By reusing plastic waste that is already in Hawaii, we can reduce the environmental and economic impacts of transporting waste plastics from the islands, incinerating it or dumping it in Hawaii's overflowing landfills.” Since 2020, most Hawaiian roads have been built with polymer-modified asphalt (PMA), which incorporates styrene-butadiene-styrene (SBS) to improve flexibility and resistance to cracking and water damage — crucial in the tropical climate. The Hawaii Department of Transportation (HDOT) partnered with CMDR director Jennifer Lynch to see if some of that virgin polymer could be swapped for recycled plastic. Lynch's team tackled two tasks. First, they supplied derelict fishing nets collected through CMDR's Bounty Project, which pays commercial fishers to remove marine debris; the project has already pulled 84 tons of gear from the Pacific. Second, they analyzed whether recycled-plastic roads shed more microplastics than standard PMA. A U.S. company processed the recovered plastics into asphalt-compatible materials, and a local paving company resurfaced sections of an Oahu residential street with three mixtures: standard SBS, recycled polyethylene from curbside recycling, and polyethylene from fishing nets. After 11 months, Lynch's team collected road dust and used pyrolysis gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (Py-GC-MS) to identify polymer types. The results were striking. Pavement containing recycled polyethylene did not release more polymers than conventional SBS pavement. In fact, tire wear particles swamped the signal from polyethylene “by orders of magnitude, like gigantic peaks!” Lynch said. “We had to search the weeds of the chromatogram to find signs of polyethylene.” The researchers believe the plastic becomes blended into the asphalt binder, so as the road wears, particles that break off are composites of rock, binder, and polymer — not pure plastic. This finding is significant because it suggests that incorporating ocean plastics into roads could be a safe, scalable way to repurpose waste without exacerbating microplastic pollution. The team is continuing to monitor the test sections and analyze stormwater runoff, but the early data offer a promising path toward turning a pollution problem into durable infrastructure.
why_it_matters: This research shows how creative engineering can tackle two problems at once: reducing plastic waste and building durable roads. If successful at scale, this method could help island communities worldwide turn trash into treasure while protecting marine ecosystems.

background_read: Hawaii sits near the Great Pacific Garbage Patch, a swirling accumulation of plastic waste, and trade winds carry tons of lost fishing nets and debris onto its shores each year.

The Center for Marine Debris Research (CMDR) at Hawaiʻi Pacific University (a private university with a strong marine science focus) studies this pollution. The Hawaii Department of Transportation (HDOT), which manages the state's roads, has been using polymer-modified asphalt since 2020.
At the American Chemical Society (the world’s largest scientific society of chemists, founded in 1876) meeting, researchers shared their progress.
Article_Structure: LEAD: Contrast of pristine beaches and plastic waste.
└─ PROBLEM: Recycling is costly, marine debris overwhelming.
SOLUTION PITCH: Using recycled plastics in roads.
├─ WHO: Jeremy Axworthy / CMDR / Hawaiʻi Pacific University.
└─ PARTNERS: HDOT, CMDR director Jennifer Lynch.
BACKGROUND: Hawaiian roads use PMA with SBS.
└─ GOAL: Swap virgin polymer with recycled plastic.
EXPERIMENT: Two tasks — supply fishing nets via Bounty Project, analyze microplastic shedding.
└─ TEST SECTION: Oahu street with three mixtures.
└─ SURPRISE RESULT: Tire wear dominates; recycled polyethylene signal nearly undetectable.
INSIGHT: Plastic blends into asphalt binder, forming composite particles.
└─ IMPLICATIONS: Safe repurposing of ocean plastics without extra microplastic pollution, ongoing monitoring.

perspectives.description: Environmentalists and engineers see a win-win situation: removing dangerous fishing nets from the ocean and using them to strengthen roads reduces both landfall and pollution. Local economies save money on importing new materials.

Skeptics worry that long-term wear could still release microplastics into stormwater runoff, potentially harming coral reefs. Also, not all plastic types are suitable, and mixing them might affect road durability over time.

The study carefully compares recycled and virgin polymer using advanced chemical analysis. The finding that tire particles dominate the microplastic signal underscores that roads already generate pollution, and replacing virgin polymer with waste does not seem to make it worse.

If ongoing monitoring confirms no increase in harmful runoff, HDOT could expand the use of ocean plastics to major highways. Other isolated regions, like islands and remote coastal communities, might follow suit, creating a global model for turning marine debris into infrastructure.
